blocks.text: Integration as the inverse of differentiation

If $\dfrac{d}{dx}F(x)=f(x)$, then $F$ is an **antiderivative** of $f$, and we write $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C$. The constant $C$ is the **constant of integration**: two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant, because the derivative of a constant is $0$.

Integration undoes differentiation. To check any integral, differentiate your answer; you must get back the integrand. Geometrically, $F(x)+C$ is a **family of curves**, each obtained from another by shifting up or down.
What to learn from this figure: All the curves have the same derivative 2x, so every one is an antiderivative of 2x. The integral therefore gives a whole family, which is why +C is needed.
Linearity: constants come out of the integral and a sum may be integrated term by term.
Integration by substitution
If an integrand has the form $f(g(x))\,g'(x)$, put $t=g(x)$ so that $dt=g'(x)\,dx$. The integral becomes $\int f(t)\,dt$, which is simpler. Return to $x$ at the end for an indefinite integral.
A very common pattern: the numerator is the derivative of the denominator. Example: $\int\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx=\ln(x^2+1)+C$.

blocks.solution: Let $t=x^2$, so $dt=2x\,dx$. The integral becomes $\int\cos t\,dt=\sin t+C=\sin(x^2)+C$. Check: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2)=2x\cos(x^2)$.

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: Look for an inner function (x^2) whose derivative (2x) is also present. Replace both with t and dt, integrate in t, then go back to x, and check by differentiating.
Integration by partial fractions
A rational function $\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ with $\deg P<\deg Q$ is split into simpler fractions according to the factors of $Q(x)$. If $\deg P\ge\deg Q$, divide first.

blocks.solution: Write $\dfrac{1}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x-2}$. Then $1=A(x-2)+B(x-1)$. Put $x=1$: $1=-A$, so $A=-1$. Put $x=2$: $1=B$. So the integral is $\int\left(\dfrac{1}{x-2}-\dfrac{1}{x-1}\right)dx=\ln|x-2|-\ln|x-1|+C=\ln\left|\dfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|+C$.

blocks.text: Integration by parts
Product rule in reverse. Choose $u$ using **ILATE**: Inverse trigonometric, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential, in that order of preference for $u$. The other factor is $v$.
A shortcut that avoids parts when the integrand has this pair structure.

blocks.solution: By ILATE, take $u=x$ (algebraic) and $v=e^x$. Then $\int xe^x\,dx=x e^x-\int 1\cdot e^x\,dx=xe^x-e^x+C=e^x(x-1)+C$.
Write $\ln x=\ln x\cdot1$ with $u=\ln x$, $v=1$. Then $\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-\int\dfrac1x\cdot x\,dx=x\ln x-x+C$.

blocks.text: Common mistake: forgetting the constant $C$ in an indefinite integral, or applying parts with the wrong choice of $u$ (for example $u=e^x$, $v=x$ makes the integral harder). Choose $u$ as the factor that becomes simpler on differentiation.
Standard integrals with a^2 and x^2
Valid for $a\ne0$ and all real $x$.
Valid for $|x|<|a|$.
The second needs $|x|>|a|$.
Derived by partial fractions: $\dfrac1{a^2-x^2}=\dfrac1{2a}\left(\dfrac1{a+x}+\dfrac1{a-x}\right)$.
Integrals involving a quadratic ax^2 + bx + c

To integrate $\dfrac1{ax^2+bx+c}$ or $\dfrac1{\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}}$, take out $a$ and **complete the square**: $ax^2+bx+c=a\left[\left(x+\dfrac b{2a}\right)^2+\dfrac{4ac-b^2}{4a^2}\right]$. Then the integral reduces to one of the standard forms with $t=x+\dfrac b{2a}$.

For $\dfrac{px+q}{ax^2+bx+c}$ or $\dfrac{px+q}{\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}}$, write the numerator as $px+q=A\,\dfrac{d}{dx}(ax^2+bx+c)+B=A(2ax+b)+B$. The $A$-part is an $f'/f$ integral (a logarithm, or a square root for the root case), and the $B$-part is a standard form after completing the square.

blocks.solution: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2+4x+5)=2x+4$. Write $2x+3=(2x+4)-1$. Then $\int\dfrac{2x+3}{x^2+4x+5}dx=\int\dfrac{2x+4}{x^2+4x+5}dx-\int\dfrac{dx}{x^2+4x+5}$. The first part is $\ln(x^2+4x+5)$. For the second, $x^2+4x+5=(x+2)^2+1$, so $\int\dfrac{dx}{(x+2)^2+1}=\tan^{-1}(x+2)$.
Complete the square: $5-4x-x^2=9-(x^2+4x+4)=9-(x+2)^2$. So the integral is $\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{3^2-(x+2)^2}}=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x+2}{3}+C$.

blocks.text: Integrals of square roots of quadratics
Derived by parts. Geometrically, a definite version gives areas of circular regions.
Note the plus sign before the logarithm term.
Note the minus sign before the logarithm term. Valid for $|x|>|a|$.

For $\int\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}\,dx$, first complete the square to get $a\left[\left(x+\dfrac b{2a}\right)^2\pm k^2\right]$, take $\sqrt a$ outside, and apply the matching standard formula with $t=x+\dfrac b{2a}$.
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

**Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (without proof).** If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $F$ is any antiderivative of $f$, then $\displaystyle\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$. The value does not depend on which antiderivative is used, because the constant $C$ cancels. The first part says $\dfrac{d}{dx}\int_a^xf(t)\,dt=f(x)$.
What to learn from this figure: A definite integral is the limit of sums of thin strips. As the strips get narrower, the lower and upper sums close in on the same number, the area 8/3.

blocks.solution: By parts with $u=\ln x$, $v=x$: $\int x\ln x\,dx=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\int\dfrac1x\cdot\dfrac{x^2}2dx=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4$. At $x=e$: $\dfrac{e^2}2-\dfrac{e^2}4=\dfrac{e^2}4$. At $x=1$: $0-\dfrac14=-\dfrac14$. So the value is $\dfrac{e^2}4-\left(-\dfrac14\right)=\dfrac{e^2+1}4$.

blocks.text: Properties of definite integrals

blocks.caption: Properties used to evaluate definite integrals
rows: $\int_{-a}^af(x)dx=2\int_0^af(x)dx$ if $f$ is even, and $0$ if $f$ is odd

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: This is property P7: for an even function the integral from -a to a is twice the integral from 0 to a; for an odd function the two halves cancel to 0.

blocks.solution: Using P5, $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin(\pi/2-x)}{\sin(\pi/2-x)+\cos(\pi/2-x)}dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x+\sin x}dx$. Adding the two forms: $2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{\sin x+\cos x}dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\dfrac\pi2$. So $I=\dfrac\pi4$.

Using the formula with $a=3$: $\left[\dfrac x2\sqrt{9-x^2}+\dfrac92\sin^{-1}\dfrac x3\right]_0^3=\left(0+\dfrac92\cdot\dfrac\pi2\right)-0=\dfrac{9\pi}4$. (This is the area of a quarter circle of radius $3$, namely $\dfrac14\pi\cdot9$.)

blocks.text: Always check an indefinite integral by differentiating. For a definite integral, do not forget to change the limits if you substitute (new limits for $t$), or return to $x$ before applying the original limits.

Decide the method by the integrand: derivative present $\Rightarrow$ substitution; rational with factorable denominator $\Rightarrow$ partial fractions; product of different kinds of function $\Rightarrow$ parts; quadratic under or in a root $\Rightarrow$ complete the square.

Exam tip: for $\int\dfrac{dx}{a^2-x^2}$ the logarithm is $\dfrac1{2a}\ln\left|\dfrac{a+x}{a-x}\right|$, and for $\int\dfrac{dx}{x^2-a^2}$ it is $\dfrac1{2a}\ln\left|\dfrac{x-a}{x+a}\right|$. The order of $a\pm x$ flips with the sign of $x^2$.

diagrams.caption: Why the constant C: a family of antiderivatives
diagrams.description: The curves y = x^2 + C for C = -2, -1, 0, 1 and 2 are copies of one parabola shifted up or down. At x = 1 the tangent to every curve (amber) is parallel, with slope 2x = 2.

diagrams.alt: A flow of boxes for the integral of 2x cos(x^2) dx from substitution t = x^2 to the result sin(x^2) + C and a check by differentiation
diagrams.caption: Integration by substitution step by step
diagrams.description: Start with the integral of 2x cos(x^2) dx. Let t = x^2 so that dt = 2x dx. The new integral is the integral of cos t dt, which is sin t + C. Replace t by x^2 to get sin(x^2) + C. The check d/dx sin(x^2) = cos(x^2) x 2x confirms it.

diagrams.alt: Two pictures of y = x^2 on 0 to 2 with 8 strips, one using left end heights and one using right end heights
diagrams.caption: Area under y = x^2 squeezed between left-end and right-end strips
diagrams.description: With n = 8 strips, the left-end strips lie below the curve and add up to 2.1875, and the right-end strips lie above the curve and add up to 3.1875. The exact area of the integral from 0 to 2 of x^2 dx is 8/3, about 2.6667, which lies between them. With n = 200 strips the bounds are 2.6467 and 2.6867.

diagrams.alt: Two graphs over -2 to 2, the even function x^2 with equal shaded halves and the odd function x^3 with a positive right half and a negative left half
diagrams.caption: Even and odd functions over limits -a to a
diagrams.description: (a) y = x^2 is even: both halves have area 8/3, so the integral from -2 to 2 is 2 x 8/3 = 16/3, about 5.333. (b) y = x^3 is odd: the right half has signed area +4 and the left half -4, so the integral from -2 to 2 is 0. The signed areas were computed numerically.

questions.stem: Term by term: $\displaystyle\int(3x^2+2x+1)\,dx=$
questions.explanation: Integrate term by term with $\int x^n\,dx=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$: $\int3x^2dx=x^3$, $\int2x\,dx=x^2$, $\int1\,dx=x$. Adding the constant, the result is $x^3+x^2+x+C$. Differentiating gives $3x^2+2x+1$, confirming it.

optionRationale.2: This is the derivative of the integrand, not its integral.
optionRationale.3: The constant of integration C is missing in an indefinite integral.
optionRationale.4: The powers are raised but the coefficients are not divided by the new power.

questions.objective: Integrate a polynomial

questions.stem: Plus sign under the denominator: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2+9}=$
questions.explanation: Here $x^2+9=x^2+3^2$, so $a=3$ in the standard result $\int\dfrac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\dfrac1a\tan^{-1}\dfrac xa+C$. Hence the integral is $\dfrac13\tan^{-1}\dfrac x3+C$.

optionRationale.4: That form belongs to 1/(x squared minus 9); here the sign is plus, giving tan inverse.

questions.objective: Use the standard tan inverse integral

questions.stem: Root of a squared minus x squared: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{16-x^2}}=$
questions.explanation: With $a=4$, $\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}\dfrac xa+C$ gives $\sin^{-1}\dfrac x4+C$. Check: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}\dfrac x4=\dfrac{1/4}{\sqrt{1-x^2/16}}=\dfrac1{\sqrt{16-x^2}}$.

optionRationale.1: The argument must be x/a = x/4.
optionRationale.2: There is no 1/a factor in the sin inverse formula.
optionRationale.4: The logarithm form is for roots of x squared plus or minus a squared.

questions.objective: Use the standard sin inverse integral

questions.stem: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $\displaystyle\int_0^1(2x+3)\,dx=$
questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus we first find any antiderivative of the integrand. Here $F(x)=x^2+3x$ works, since its derivative is $2x+3$. Then $\int_0^1(2x+3)dx=F(1)-F(0)=(1+3)-0=4$. The constant of integration cancels in the difference, so it is not needed.

optionRationale.1: Only the constant term was integrated; the x squared term gives 1 as well.
optionRationale.2: This evaluates the integrand 2x + 3 at x = 1 instead of the antiderivative.
optionRationale.3: This is the derivative of the integrand 2x + 3, not its definite integral.

questions.objective: Evaluate a simple definite integral

questions.stem: Trigonometric integrand: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=$
questions.explanation: An antiderivative of $\sin x$ is $-\cos x$, because the derivative of $-\cos x$ is $\sin x$. So $\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx=[-\cos x]_0^\pi=(-\cos\pi)-(-\cos0)=1+1=2$. This is also the area under one arch of the sine curve, which is positive.

optionRationale.2: This would be the result over a full period 0 to 2 pi, where positive and negative areas cancel.
optionRationale.3: The antiderivative of sin x is -cos x; evaluating -cos(pi) - (-cos 0) = 1 + 1 = +2.
optionRationale.4: This takes only cos 0 = 1; the second term cos(pi) = -1 also contributes.

questions.objective: Evaluate a trigonometric definite integral

questions.stem: Integration by parts: $\displaystyle\int x\,e^{x}\,dx=$
questions.explanation: By parts with $u=x$, $v=e^x$: $\int xe^xdx=xe^x-\int e^xdx=xe^x-e^x+C=e^x(x-1)+C$. Differentiating: $e^x(x-1)+e^x=xe^x$, as required.

optionRationale.1: Differentiating this gives e^x(x+2), not x e^x; the sign inside the bracket is wrong.
optionRationale.3: This treats x and e^x as separate integrals multiplied together, which is not valid.
optionRationale.4: Its derivative is e^x(x+1), so the integral is missing the term -e^x.

questions.objective: Integrate by parts using ILATE

questions.stem: Partial fractions: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}=$
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1{(x-1)(x-2)}=\dfrac{1}{x-2}-\dfrac1{x-1}$ (check: combined numerator $(x-1)-(x-2)=1$). Integrating gives $\ln|x-2|-\ln|x-1|+C=\ln\left|\dfrac{x-2}{x-1}\right|+C$.

optionRationale.1: The ratio is inverted; the sign of the partial fractions (A = -1, B = +1) was reversed.
optionRationale.2: The integral of 1/(product) is not the log of the product.
optionRationale.4: The factor 1/2 belongs to the 1/(a squared - x squared) form; here the roots differ by 1.

questions.objective: Integrate a rational function by partial fractions

questions.stem: Complete the square: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2+2x+5}=$
questions.explanation: Complete the square: $x^2+2x+5=(x+1)^2+4=(x+1)^2+2^2$. With $t=x+1$ and $a=2$, the integral is $\dfrac1a\tan^{-1}\dfrac ta+C=\dfrac12\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+1}2+C$.

optionRationale.1: x squared + 2x + 5 = (x+1) squared + 4 so a = 2, not 1.
optionRationale.2: The completed square gives x + 1 in the argument, not x.
optionRationale.3: The constant after completing the square is 4 = 2 squared, not 5.

questions.objective: Complete the square and apply the tan inverse form

questions.stem: Coefficient in a standard result: $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{x^2-16}\,dx=\dfrac x2\sqrt{x^2-16}-k\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-16}\right|+C$. The value of $k$ is
questions.explanation: The standard result is $\int\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\,dx=\dfrac x2\sqrt{x^2-a^2}-\dfrac{a^2}2\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right|+C$. Here $a^2=16$, so $k=\dfrac{16}2=8$.

optionRationale.2: The coefficient is a squared over 2, i.e. 16/2.
optionRationale.3: This is a, not a squared over 2.
optionRationale.4: This is a squared divided by 8, not by 2.

questions.objective: Recall the coefficient in the integral of sqrt(x^2 - a^2)

questions.stem:
Consider the following standard integrals (constants of integration omitted).
A. $\int\dfrac{dx}{a^2-x^2}=\dfrac1{2a}\ln\left|\dfrac{a+x}{a-x}\right|$
B. $\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}=\sin^{-1}\dfrac xa$
C. $\int\dfrac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\dfrac1a\tan^{-1}\dfrac xa$
D. $\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}\dfrac xa$
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A is correct (obtained by partial fractions). B is wrong: the integral of $1/\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ is $\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right|$; sin inverse belongs to $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$. C is correct. D is correct. So A, C and D are correct.

optionRationale.2: It includes B, which is false, and omits D.
optionRationale.3: It includes B, which is false, and omits A.
optionRationale.4: C is also correct, so this selection is incomplete.

questions.objective: Verify standard integral formulas

questions.stem: Match the integrals in List-I with their results (constant omitted) in List-II.
questions.explanation: $\int\dfrac{dx}{x^2+4}=\dfrac12\tan^{-1}\dfrac x2$ (II). $\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}\dfrac x2$ (I). $\int\dfrac{dx}{4-x^2}=\dfrac14\ln\left|\dfrac{2+x}{2-x}\right|$ with $a=2$ (III). $\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-4}}=\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-4}\right|$ (IV). Hence A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

optionRationale.2: It swaps the tan inverse and sin inverse results for A and B.
optionRationale.3: It swaps the two logarithmic results for C and D.
optionRationale.4: It assigns the logarithmic result of C to A, which contains no root and has a plus sign (tan inverse).

questions.objective: Match integrals of a squared and x squared forms with results

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}x^3\,dx=0$.
Reason (R): For an odd function $f$, $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=0$.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: $f(x)=x^3$ is odd, since $f(-x)=-f(x)$. For odd functions the area on the left of the origin cancels that on the right, so $\int_{-a}^af=0$. Direct check: $\left[\dfrac{x^4}4\right]_{-2}^2=4-4=0$. R is true and explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is the exact property that gives A, so it is the explanation.
optionRationale.3: R is true: it is the standard property of odd functions.
optionRationale.4: A is true, as the direct calculation 4 - 4 = 0 shows.

questions.objective: Use the odd function property of definite integrals

questions.stem: Substitution: $\displaystyle\int 2x\cos\left(x^2\right)dx=$
questions.explanation: Put $t=x^2$, so $dt=2x\,dx$. The integral becomes $\int\cos t\,dt=\sin t+C=\sin\left(x^2\right)+C$. Differentiating the answer gives $\cos(x^2)\cdot2x$, which matches the integrand.

optionRationale.1: This is not the antiderivative; x sin(x squared) differentiates to something else entirely.
optionRationale.2: The integral of cos t is +sin t, with no minus sign.
optionRationale.4: Substitution t = x squared absorbs the factor 2x dx = dt; it does not remain outside.

questions.objective: Use substitution when the derivative of the inner function is present

questions.stem: Derivative of the denominator in the numerator: $\displaystyle\int\frac{2x+3}{x^2+4x+5}\,dx=$
questions.explanation: The derivative of the denominator is $2x+4$, so write $2x+3=(2x+4)-1$. Then $\int\dfrac{2x+4}{x^2+4x+5}dx=\ln(x^2+4x+5)$ and $\int\dfrac{dx}{(x+2)^2+1}=\tan^{-1}(x+2)$. So the result is $\ln(x^2+4x+5)-\tan^{-1}(x+2)+C$.

optionRationale.1: Writing 2x + 3 = (2x + 4) - 1 gives a minus sign in front of the tan inverse term.
optionRationale.3: The log term has coefficient 1 because 2x + 4 is exactly the derivative of the denominator.
optionRationale.4: The completed square is (x+2) squared + 1, so the argument of tan inverse is x + 2.

questions.objective: Split (px + q) over a quadratic into derivative and constant parts

questions.stem: Completing the square under a root: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{5-4x-x^2}}=$

optionRationale.1: Completing the square gives 9 - (x+2) squared, so a = 3, not root 5.
optionRationale.2: The completed square is (x + 2) squared, so the shift is +2.
optionRationale.4: The quantity under the root is of the form a squared minus t squared, so the result is sin inverse, not a logarithm.

questions.objective: Complete the square under a square root

questions.stem: Quarter-circle type: $\displaystyle\int_0^3\sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx=$
questions.explanation: With $a=3$: $\left[\dfrac x2\sqrt{9-x^2}+\dfrac92\sin^{-1}\dfrac x3\right]_0^3$. At $3$: $0+\dfrac92\cdot\dfrac\pi2=\dfrac{9\pi}4$. At $0$: $0$. So the value is $\dfrac{9\pi}4$, equal to a quarter of the area $9\pi$ of the circle $x^2+y^2=9$.

optionRationale.1: This is the area of a semicircle of radius 3; the integral from 0 to 3 is only a quarter circle.
optionRationale.2: This uses a instead of a squared in the coefficient a squared over 2.
optionRationale.3: This is the area of the full circle of radius 3.

questions.objective: Evaluate a definite integral of a square root of a squared minus x squared

questions.stem: Repeated parts: $\displaystyle\int x^2e^x\,dx=$
questions.explanation: Apply parts twice. First, $\int x^2e^xdx=x^2e^x-\int2xe^xdx$. Then $\int2xe^xdx=2e^x(x-1)$. So the result is $x^2e^x-2e^x(x-1)=e^x(x^2-2x+2)$, plus $C$. Differentiating: $e^x(x^2-2x+2)+e^x(2x-2)=x^2e^x$.

optionRationale.2: Differentiating gives e^x(x^2+4x+4), not x^2 e^x; the signs alternate in repeated parts.
optionRationale.3: The final constant term +2 is missing; the derivative would be e^x(x^2-2), not x^2 e^x.
optionRationale.4: The product of two functions cannot be integrated by integrating each separately.

questions.objective: Apply integration by parts twice

questions.stem: King property of definite integrals: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx=$
questions.explanation: Let $I$ be the integral. By the property $\int_0^af(x)dx=\int_0^af(a-x)dx$, $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x+\sin x}dx$. Adding the two forms, $2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\dfrac\pi2$, so $I=\dfrac\pi4$.

optionRationale.1: This would be the integral of 1; the two similar integrals add up to pi/2, so each is half.
optionRationale.3: Halving twice; the two integrals sum to pi/2, so each is pi/4.
optionRationale.4: This is the value of integral of sin x alone from 0 to pi/2; the given integrand is different.

questions.objective: Apply the property of definite integrals int f(x) = int f(a-x)

questions.stem: Exponential-pattern integral: $\displaystyle\int e^x\left(\frac1x-\frac1{x^2}\right)dx=$
questions.explanation: Let $f(x)=\dfrac1x$. Then $f'(x)=-\dfrac1{x^2}$, so the integrand is $e^x[f(x)+f'(x)]$. By $\int e^x[f+f']dx=e^xf$, the integral is $\dfrac{e^x}x+C$. Check: $\dfrac d{dx}\dfrac{e^x}x=\dfrac{e^x}x-\dfrac{e^x}{x^2}$.

optionRationale.1: The pattern e^x [f + f prime] has f = 1/x, so the result is e^x f = e^x / x.
optionRationale.2: This is not the antiderivative; its derivative is e^x ln x + e^x / x.
optionRationale.4: The sign is wrong: f(x) = 1/x with f prime = -1/x squared gives +e^x / x.

questions.objective: Recognise the e^x[f(x)+f prime(x)] pattern

questions.stem: Parts with a logarithm over limits: $\displaystyle\int_1^e x\ln x\,dx=$
questions.explanation: By parts, $\int x\ln x\,dx=\dfrac{x^2}2\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}4$. At $e$: $\dfrac{e^2}2-\dfrac{e^2}4=\dfrac{e^2}4$. At $1$: $0-\dfrac14$. Hence $\int_1^ex\ln x\,dx=\dfrac{e^2}4+\dfrac14=\dfrac{e^2+1}4\approx2.097$.

optionRationale.1: The lower limit contributes -(0 - 1/4) = +1/4, so the numerator is e squared + 1.
optionRationale.2: The -x squared/4 part of the antiderivative has been dropped.
optionRationale.3: The antiderivative is x squared/2 ln x - x squared/4; the denominator is 4, not 2.

questions.objective: Evaluate a definite integral using integration by parts
